1.q: what was right in the eyes of Yahweh
1.note: The eyes here represent seeing, and seeing represents judgment. Yahweh saw and did not approve of Ahaz’s actions. See how you translated this in 2 Chronicles 14:2. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh judged to be right] or [what Yahweh considered to be right]

2.q: he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel
2.note: Walking represents behavior and actions. Alternate translation: [he acted the same way that the kings of Israel had acted] or [he did the things that the kings of Israel had done]

3.note: This is a valley in Jerusalem.

The people of those nations fled as the people of Israel moved into the land. The full meaning of this statement can be made explicit. Alternate translation: [before the people of Israel who moved into the land] or [as the people of Israel moved into the land]

4.q: the high places and on the hills and under every green tree
4.note: These are places where the people of the other nations worshiped their false gods.

God wanted his people to offer sacrifices to him in Jerusalem. The word “every” here is an exaggeration to show how determined King Ahaz was to disobey God by offering sacrifices in many other places instead. Alternate translation: [under many green trees] or [under many green trees around the country]

5.q: Yahweh the God of Ahaz gave him into the hand of the king of Aram
5.note: Here the metonym “hand” represents power. God enabling the army of the king of Aram to defeat Ahaz and his army is spoken of as if God had put Ahaz in the hand of the king of Aram. Alternate translation: [Yahweh the God of Ahaz enabled the king of Aram to defeat Ahaz] (See also: [Metaphor](ta:figs-metaphor))
“carried away from Ahaz.” Here “him” represents Ahaz’s army. Alternate translation: [carried away from Ahaz’s army]

5.q: Ahaz was also given into the hand of the king of Israel who defeated him
5.note: Here the metonym “hand” represents power. God enabling the army of the king of Israel to defeat Ahaz and his army is spoken of as if God had put Ahaz in the hand of the king of Israel. If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh also enabled the king of Israel to defeat Ahaz] (See also: [Metaphor](ta:figs-metaphor); and [Active or Passive](ta:figs-activepassive))

6.note: This was the king of Israel. Both “Pekah” and “Remaliah” are the names of men.

7.note: These are the names of men.
This is an idiom that refers to a mighty warrior. Alternate translation: [a mighty warrior]

7.q: who was next to the king
7.note: This idiom means that this man was the king’s assistant who was second in command. Alternate translation: [who was the king’s second in command]

8.q: The army of Israel took captive from their relatives
8.note: “From their own relatives, the army of Israel took captive.” The word “their” refers to the army of Israel. The narrator speaks of the people of Judah as the relatives of the people of Israel.
“two hundred thousand wives, sons, and daughters”

9.note: This is the name of a man.

9.q: he gave them into your hand
9.note: Here the word “hand” represents power. God enabling the army of Israel to defeat the army of Judah is spoken of as if God had put the army of Judah in the hand of the army of Israel. Alternate translation: [God enabled you to defeat them] (See also: [Metaphor](ta:figs-metaphor))

9.q: you have slaughtered them in a rage that reached up to heaven
9.note: Oded speaks of Yahweh knowing how severely the army of Israel slaughtered the army of Judah as if the rage with which the army of Israel slaughtered them were an object so large that it reached into heaven. That Yahweh knows what they have done implies that he will respond. Alternate translation: [you have slaughtered them in such great rage that Yahweh himself has noticed and will take vengeance] (See also: [Assumed Knowledge and Implicit Information](ta:figs-explicit))

10.q: But are you not guilty of sins of your own against Yahweh your God?
10.note: Oded asks this rhetorical question to rebuke the army of Israel and to emphasize the positive answer that the question anticipates. Alternate translation: [But you yourselves are guilty of sins of your own against Yahweh your God.]

11.q: Yahweh’s fierce wrath is on you
11.note: Oded speaks of Yahweh being extremely angry with the Israelite army as if Yahweh’s wrath were an object that were upon them. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is extremely angry with you]

12.q: Azariah son of Jehohanan, Berechiah son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah son of Shallum, and Amasa son of Hadlai
12.note: These are all names of men.

12.q: stood up against those who came back from the war
12.note: The phrase “stood up against” is an idiom that means to confront or to oppose. Alternate translation: [confronted those who came back from the war] or [opposed those who came back from the war]

13.q: something that will bring on us sin
13.note: The leaders speak of doing something that will cause them to be guilty of sin as if it were sin were an object that the action brings upon them. Alternate translation: [something that will cause us to be guilty of sinning]

13.q: there is fierce wrath against Israel
13.note: This phrase implies that it is Yahweh’s fierce wrath that is against Israel. The words “fierce wrath” can be translated with a verbal phrase. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is extremely angry with the people of Israel] (See also: [Abstract Nouns](ta:figs-abstractnouns))

15.q: The men who were assigned by name
15.note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [The men whom the leaders assigned by name]
This is a type of shoe.

15.q: put the weak ones on donkeys
15.note: Alternate translation: [put the weak ones who were too weak to walk on donkeys]

18.note: Taking a city is an idiom that means to conquer or to capture the city. Alternate translation: [The Philistines captured Beth Shemesh]

18.q: Beth Shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, Soko … Timnah … Gimzo
18.note: These are the names of places.

19.q: Yahweh brought Judah low because of Ahaz
19.note: The metonym “Judah” represents the people of Judah. Yahweh humiliating the people is spoken of as if he physically brought Judah low to the ground. Alternate translation: [Yahweh humiliated the people of Judah because of Ahaz] (See also: [Metaphor](ta:figs-metaphor))
Ahaz sinning very much is spoken of as if sin were a very heavy object. Alternate translation: [sinned very greatly against Yahweh]

20.note: This is Tiglath-Pileser III, also known as Pul.

20.q: troubled him instead of strengthening him
20.note: Helping Ahaz against his enemies is spoken of as if it were strengthening Ahaz. Alternate translation: [caused him trouble instead of helping him]

23.note: The Syrians believed Damascus to be the city where their gods dwelt, much like Yahweh dwelt in Jerusalem. Alternate translation: [the gods whom the Syrians worshiped in Damascus]

This expresses Ahaz’s opinion. Because the Syrians had defeated him and his army, Ahaz attributed his defeat to the gods whom the Syrians worshiped. Alternate translation: [gods whom he believed had enabled the Syrian army to defeat him]

23.q: they were the ruin of him and of all Israel
23.note: The word “ruin” can be translated with a verb. Alternate translation: [those gods ruined him and all Israel]
Here “Israel” represents the southern kingdom of Judah.

24.q: the house of God … the house of Yahweh
24.note: Here the word “house” represents the temple. Alternate translation: [the temple of God … the temple of Yahweh]

This could mean: (1) the word “corner” refers to street corners, or places where streets intersect. Alternate translation: [on every street corner in Jerusalem] or (2) the various parts of Jerusalem are spoken of as if they were the corners of the city. Alternate translation: [in every part of Jerusalem]
Since Ahaz was king, he may have had his workers make these high places. Alternate translation: [he had his workers make altars for him]

25.q: he made high places to burn sacrifices
25.note: Since Ahaz was king, he may have had his workers make these high places. Alternate translation: [he had his workers make high places to burn sacrifices]

26.q: all his ways, first and last
26.note: Ahaz’s actions are spoken of as if they were a path upon which he walked. The phrase “first and last” refers to those extremes and everything in between. Alternate translation: [all that he did from the beginning of his reign to the end of his reign] (See also: [Merism](ta:figs-merism))

26.q: see, they are written in the book … Israel
26.note: Alternate translation: [anyone can look at the book … Israel and see that they are written there]

26.q: they are written in the book
26.note: If your language does not use the passive form in this way, you can state this in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [someone has written them in the book] or [you can read of them in the book]

26.q: the book of the kings of Judah and Israel
26.note: This is a book that no longer exists.

27.note: Ahaz dying is spoken of as if he had fallen asleep. Alternate translation: [Ahaz died] (See also: [Euphemism](ta:figs-euphemism))
The phrase “in his place” is a metaphor meaning “instead of him.” Alternate translation: [became king instead of Ahaz]
